questions.explanation: 802.11n uses multiple antennas and separately processed data streams to improve wireless transfer capacity.

questions.prompt: What capability distinguishes multiuser MIMO in the chapter?
options: It prevents all reflection in a room
An AP can transmit to multiple client stations simultaneously
It removes the need for client antennas
It converts every WLAN into a token ring
questions.explanation: MU-MIMO supports simultaneous transmissions to multiple clients, with beamforming directing signals toward receiving devices.

questions.prompt: Which additional frequency band does the chapter associate with Wi-Fi 6E?
options: 900 MHz
60 GHz
1 GHz
6 GHz
questions.explanation: The chapter describes Wi-Fi 6E as extending Wi-Fi 6 operation to the 6 GHz band.

questions.prompt: What channel-width change does the chapter describe for Wi-Fi 7 in the 6 GHz band?
options: Channels can be 320 MHz wide
Channels are restricted to 5 MHz
Channels shrink to 1 MHz
Channel width becomes unrelated to bandwidth
questions.explanation: The chapter describes doubling channel width to 320 MHz in the 6 GHz band for Wi-Fi 7.

questions.prompt: Which statements explain the need for Wi-Fi security and compatible encryption settings? Select all correct answers.
options: Radio signals stop at a building's exterior walls
WEP is the strongest protocol listed in the chapter
Devices outside a building may detect its wireless signals
Clients must support the encryption protocol configured on the AP
questions.explanation: Wireless signals can extend beyond the intended space. The AP and clients need compatible protection, and the chapter identifies WEP as weak.

questions.prompt: Why can a Wi-Fi link's advertised rate be much higher than its useful file-transfer rate?
questions.exampleAnswer: Interference, errors, retransmissions, and acknowledgments reduce actual throughput. Packet and frame headers also consume capacity without carrying file content. Goodput counts only application data delivered over time, so it can be lower than both the rated rate and throughput.

questions.prompt: Which combination describes token ring as presented in the chapter?
options: IEEE 802.3 with a physical bus and logical star
IEEE 802.11 with a physical mesh and logical bus
IEEE 802.5 with a physical star and logical ring
IEEE 802.3 with a physical ring and logical mesh
questions.explanation: Token ring follows IEEE 802.5 and typically uses an MAU to create a logical ring within physical star cabling.

questions.prompt: In token-passing access, which station may transmit data?
options: Every station as soon as it has data
The station currently holding the token
Only the station nearest the central device
The station with the lowest MAC address
questions.explanation: The token grants permission to transmit for a limited time. Stations without data pass it onward.

questions.prompt: Which tradeoffs are associated with token passing? Select all correct answers.
options: Every station must resolve CSMA/CD collisions before sending
A station with data may need to wait for the token
Only the token holder transmits, preventing contention collisions
Creating and managing tokens adds equipment complexity and cost
questions.explanation: Controlled turns avoid contention collisions, but impose token-waiting time and require more complex equipment.

questions.prompt: Why did FDDI use dual rings?
options: To let Ethernet hubs operate at 10 Gbps
To eliminate all fiber-optic cabling
To provide a separate ring for each IP address
To provide redundancy if a ring path or device fails
questions.explanation: Dual rings provide an alternate path, helping overcome a single ring's vulnerability to a failure.

questions.prompt: Which description matches standard FDDI in the chapter?
options: 100 Mbps, token passing, usually dual fiber-optic rings
10 Mbps, CSMA/CD, a single coaxial bus
1 Gbps, CSMA/CA, a wireless star
100 Mbps, broadband TV channels, a coaxial tree
questions.explanation: FDDI is presented as a 100 Mbps token-passing technology with dual rings, usually using fiber-optic cabling.

questions.prompt: Explain why switched Ethernet displaced token ring and FDDI in the chapter's historical account.
questions.exampleAnswer: Ethernet delivered increasing bandwidth at lower cost. Switched full-duplex links avoided the collision delays of shared Ethernet, while token-based technologies carried greater complexity and expense. Their earlier advantages became less compelling.

questions.prompt: An office needs mobile laptop access in a second building across a street, plus access to servers in the main building. There is clear line of sight, and no wired crossing is available. Propose a topology and technology arrangement using this chapter.
questions.exampleAnswer: Use an 802.11 infrastructure WLAN with an AP for the mobile laptops. Link the buildings with a point-to-point wireless bridge, using focused antennas where appropriate. Connect the bridge and AP into the switched Ethernet LAN so laptops can reach the main-building servers. This adds an infrastructure wireless network and a point-to-point interbuilding link.

questions.prompt: During a packet-capture lab, which Ethernet header fields would you inspect to identify the sending NIC, receiving NIC, and encapsulated protocol?
questions.exampleAnswer: Inspect Source MAC Address for the sending NIC, Destination MAC Address for the intended receiving NIC or broadcast destination, and Type for the encapsulated protocol. IP addresses belong to the IP header inside the frame, not these Ethernet address fields.

questions.definition: The arrangement of network cabling and the connections that join devices.
The path or pattern that data follows as it travels between devices on a network.
A layout in which computers attach along one continuous cable segment with termination at both ends.
A layout in which each endpoint has its own cable to a central device such as a switch or hub.
A hierarchy in which a central switch connects to other switches, each serving its own group of endpoints.
A cable layout that connects devices in a closed loop, including a connection from the last device back to the first.
A direct communication link joining exactly two devices.
An arrangement in which one central device communicates with multiple other devices and their communication passes through that center.
An arrangement of interconnected devices with redundant paths, implemented with connections between all pairs or only selected pairs.
The movement of a transmitted electrical or other network signal through the communication medium.
An electrical signal reaching an unterminated cable end and traveling back along the cable, potentially interfering with later signals.
A resistive component at the end of a legacy bus cable that absorbs signals to prevent them from returning along the cable.
The high-capacity connections used to carry traffic between LANs or between switches.
A radio-based point-to-point connection that links separate networks, such as the LANs in two buildings.
A shared-media arrangement in which connected stations hear transmissions and share the available bandwidth, even when the cabling forms a star.
A logical arrangement that creates temporary forwarding paths between source and destination ports so separate device pairs can communicate concurrently.
The central device in a token ring network whose internal electronics pass data around an ordered loop and bypass unused ports.
The rules an interface uses to access a medium and send frames, often specifying frame structure and acceptable media.
LAN cabling consisting of four pairs of copper wires twisted together inside a jacket, susceptible to electrical interference.
A medium that carries pulses of light through thin glass strands, supports long distances, and is immune to electrical interference.
The cable medium used for early physical-bus Ethernet and still used for cable TV and cable-modem Internet access.
Signaling that sends digital pulses using the medium's bandwidth for one transmission, as described for Ethernet LANs.
Signaling that divides a medium into separate frequency channels so it can carry multiple signals, as in cable TV and cable Internet.
A 48-bit physical identifier of a network interface, commonly written as twelve hexadecimal digits.
The unit of network information transmitted and received by NICs and forwarded by switches, containing a header, data, and a trailer.
The four-byte Ethernet trailer field that stores an error-checking value for detecting damage in transit.
A mathematically calculated error-detection value that a receiver recomputes and compares with the transmitted value to detect altered data.
The rules governing how and when a network interface may transmit onto a communication medium.
The half-duplex Ethernet access algorithm that listens before transmitting, detects simultaneous transmissions, and retries after a random wait.
acceptedTerms: Carrier Sense Multiple Access with Collision Detection

questions.definition: An event in which two or more devices transmit simultaneously onto the same shared medium and their signals interfere.
The shared Ethernet segment or group of hub-connected segments across which interfering simultaneous transmissions can propagate, bounded by switch or router ports.
Communication in which a station can send and receive data, but cannot do both at the same time.
Communication in which a station can send and receive at the same time; on a switched Ethernet link, collision detection is unnecessary.
An Ethernet variant providing 10 Mbps over Category 3 or higher twisted-pair cabling using two wire pairs.
The common 100 Mbps twisted-pair Ethernet variant that uses two wire pairs, one for sending and one for receiving.
A 100 Mbps fiber-based Ethernet variant useful for backbone links, longer cable runs, and electrically noisy locations.
The twisted-pair Gigabit Ethernet variant that uses all four pairs and can transmit and receive on each pair simultaneously.
The paired Ethernet options providing 2.5 and 5 Gbps on existing Cat 5e/6 cabling, useful for faster access-point uplinks.
The full-duplex-only 10 Gbps twisted-pair Ethernet variant described as using four pairs of Cat 6A or Cat 7 cabling.
The IEEE 802.11 family of networking technologies that carries local network traffic using radio signals.
A location offering access to a public wireless LAN, such as a library or cafe.
A wireless operating mode in which stations connect through a central access point before communicating with other devices.
A wireless operating mode in which devices communicate directly without a central access point, often for small or temporary installations.
An antenna that covers surrounding devices in a broad pattern, typically strongest horizontally around its axis and weaker above and below it.
An antenna that focuses radio energy in one direction, useful for a narrow space or a link between buildings.
The wireless access algorithm that listens for the medium, seeks to avoid simultaneous transmissions, and uses acknowledgments and retry delays for unsuccessful exchanges.
acceptedTerms: Carrier Sense Multiple Access with Collision Avoidance

questions.definition: The 802.11 access method described as using a collision-avoidance algorithm to coordinate stations sharing the wireless medium.
A waiting interval before retrying transmission; the chapter describes a random delay after an unsuccessful wireless exchange.
A wireless condition in which clients can reach the access point but cannot hear each other, so their transmissions may interfere without mutual awareness.
The initial control message a wireless station sends to ask an access point for permission to transmit when optional handshaking is enabled.
The control reply granting a wireless station permission to transmit after it asks the access point, allowing other stations to defer.
A reduction in signal strength, such as the weakening that occurs when radio waves pass through dense material.
A process in which material takes in radio signal energy, leaving a weaker signal after it passes through the material.
The bending of a radio wave as it passes between media of different densities, changing its direction of travel.
The bending of a wave around an obstacle, which can distort the wave or redirect part of it.
The bouncing of a radio wave from a dense reflective surface, creating a copy that may follow a different path to the receiver.
The unpredictable redirection of radio energy by small irregular objects such as leaves, dust, or water droplets.
The arrival of copies of the same radio signal along different routes and at different times, potentially causing distortion.
A comparison of useful signal strength with the level of background interference affecting reception.
The actual data transfer rate after accounting for losses to errors and acknowledgments, before excluding protocol headers from the delivered data.
The rate at which useful application data is delivered, excluding protocol headers and other network overhead.
Network traffic beyond the application content, including packet and frame headers, acknowledgments, and retransmissions.
An antenna technique that uses multiple separately processed signal paths or data streams to improve wireless capacity, introduced in 802.11n.
A wireless capability that lets an access point send data to several client stations at the same time.
A technique that directs an access point's radio transmission toward a receiving device instead of spreading it uniformly in all directions.
The IEEE 802.5 LAN technology that usually uses physical star cabling while passing a special permission frame around a logical loop.
A controlled access method in which a special frame circulates between stations and only its current holder may transmit data.
A legacy 100 Mbps networking technology that uses token passing and usually two fiber-optic rings for redundancy.
